people/pseudo-dionysius/summary: Anonymous Syrian Christian writer of the late 5th or early 6th century who wrote under the name of Dionysius, Paul’s Athenian convert (Acts 17:34). His Celestial Hierarchy arranged the angels in three triads of three, and his Mystical Theology shaped apophatic theology East and West; his works were first cited by Miaphysite theologians around 532 and translated into Latin by Eriugena.
people/pseudo-dionysius/keyIdeas/0: Nine orders of angels in three triads
people/pseudo-dionysius/keyIdeas/1: Hierarchy as participation in divine light
people/evagrius-ponticus/summary: Monk of the Egyptian desert (Nitria and Kellia), disciple of the Cappadocians, who analysed spiritual combat as a struggle with eight “thoughts” (logismoi) instigated by demons — the ancestor of the seven deadly sins. Some of his Origenist speculations were condemned in 553, but his ascetic teaching shaped Eastern and Western monasticism through Cassian.
people/evagrius-ponticus/keyIdeas/1: Demons and the discernment of spirits
people/evagrius-ponticus/keyIdeas/6: The theologian is one who prays truly
people/heinrich-kramer/summary: German Dominican inquisitor who obtained Innocent VIII’s bull Summis desiderantes (1484) and wrote the Malleus Maleficarum (1486), the most notorious manual for identifying and prosecuting witches. His trials at Innsbruck (1485) were halted by the local bishop; the attribution of co-authorship to Jakob Sprenger is now widely doubted.
people/heinrich-kramer/keyIdeas/0: Witchcraft as a heresy and a conspiracy with the devil
people/friedrich-spee/summary: German Jesuit who, having ministered to accused witches facing execution in Franconia, anonymously published Cautio Criminalis (1631), a devastating critique of torture and of witch-trial procedure. He died nursing plague-stricken soldiers in Trier.
people/balthasar-bekker/summary: Dutch Reformed minister in Amsterdam whose The World Bewitched (De Betoverde Weereld, 1691), drawing on Cartesian philosophy, argued that the devil has no power to act in the material world and that belief in witchcraft and possession is unbiblical superstition. He was deposed from the ministry in 1692.
people/balthasar-bekker/keyIdeas/0: Denial of demonic agency in the world
people/increase-mather/summary: Boston Puritan minister and president of Harvard whose Cases of Conscience concerning Evil Spirits (1693) criticised the use of “spectral evidence” in the Salem trials and helped bring them to an end, though he did not deny the reality of witchcraft. He was the father of Cotton Mather.
people/walter-wink/summary: United Methodist biblical scholar at Auburn Theological Seminary whose Powers trilogy (1984-92) reinterpreted the New Testament “principalities and powers” as the inner spirituality of institutions and structures, created good, fallen, and to be redeemed, and developed a theology of active nonviolence.
people/walter-wink/keyIdeas/0: Powers as the interiority of institutions
people/derek-prince/summary: British Bible teacher born in Bangalore, educated at Cambridge, who after a Pentecostal conversion in the army (1941) became a leading international teacher of deliverance ministry in the charismatic movement, notably through They Shall Expel Demons (1998).
people/derek-prince/keyIdeas/2: Spiritual warfare through Scripture and prayer
people/emmanuel-milingo/summary: Zambian Catholic archbishop of Lusaka (1969-83) whose healing and exorcism ministry addressed African experiences of spirit affliction. Summoned to Rome in 1982 amid controversy, he resigned his see and continued a healing ministry in Italy; his later marriage (2001) and unauthorised ordinations led to his excommunication in 2006.
people/emmanuel-milingo/keyIdeas/0: Healing and exorcism in African Catholic context
people/j-denny-weaver/summary: American Mennonite theologian (Bluffton University) whose The Nonviolent Atonement (2001) proposed "narrative Christus Victor" as an atonement model without divinely sanctioned violence.
people/alexander-campbell/summary: Irish-born American reformer, founder of Bethany College, who with his father Thomas and with Barton W. Stone led the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement; he taught immersion of believers "for the remission of sins".
people/alexander-campbell/keyIdeas/2: Christian unity on the Bible alone
people/alexander-campbell/keyIdeas/4: Baptism for the remission of sins
people/james-d-g-dunn/summary: British New Testament scholar (Durham) who named the "New Perspective on Paul" (1982 Manson lecture), arguing that "works of the law" refers chiefly to Jewish boundary markers; his Baptism in the Holy Spirit (1970) argued that Spirit-baptism in the New Testament is part of conversion-initiation.
people/john-smyth/summary: English Separatist who in Amsterdam (1609) baptized himself and his congregation on profession of faith, founding the first identifiable Baptist church; he later sought union with the Waterlander Mennonites.
people/apollinaris-of-laodicea/summary: Bishop of Laodicea in Syria, scholar and friend of Athanasius, who defended Nicaea but taught that the divine Word replaced the human mind in Christ. Condemned at Constantinople (381).
people/apollinaris-of-laodicea/keyIdeas/: Word in place of human mind
people/theodore-of-mopsuestia/summary: Antiochene bishop and biblical commentator, friend of John Chrysostom, honoured in the Church of the East as ‘the Interpreter’. He emphasised the full humanity of Christ and literal-historical exegesis; condemned posthumously at Constantinople II (553).
people/eutyches/summary: Archimandrite of a large monastery in Constantinople, godfather of the eunuch Chrysaphius. His teaching that Christ's humanity was not consubstantial with ours after the union led to the Robber Synod (449) and Chalcedon (451), which condemned him.
people/sergius-of-constantinople/summary: Patriarch of Constantinople (610–638) who led the city's defence during the Avar-Persian siege of 626 and devised monoenergism and monothelitism with Emperor Heraclius to reunite the Miaphysites.
people/babai-the-great/summary: Abbot of the Great Monastery on Mount Izla and leading theologian of the Church of the East, whose Book of the Union formulated its classic Christology of two natures and two qnome in one parsopa.
people/jacob-baradaeus/summary: Bishop of Edessa, consecrated c. 542 with the backing of Empress Theodora, who travelled in disguise ordaining clergy and bishops across Syria and beyond, creating the hierarchy of the Syriac Orthodox Church (hence the name ‘Jacobite’).
people/elipandus-of-toledo/summary: Archbishop of Toledo in Muslim-ruled Spain who, with Felix of Urgell, taught that Christ in his humanity is Son of God by adoption. Condemned by Frankish synods (Regensburg 792, Frankfurt 794), though he himself remained in office under Umayyad rule.
people/gottfried-thomasius/summary: Lutheran theologian of the Erlangen school whose Christi Person und Werk (1853–61) gave the classic form of kenotic Christology.
people/charles-gore/summary: Anglican bishop of Worcester, Birmingham and Oxford and editor of Lux Mundi (1889), whose essay and Bampton Lectures (1891) introduced kenotic Christology to Anglo-Catholic theology and sought to reconcile Catholic faith with biblical criticism.
people/edward-irving/summary: Scottish preacher in London whose teaching that Christ assumed fallen human nature led to his deposition (1833); his congregation's experiences of tongues and prophecy (1831) and his premillennialism fed into the Catholic Apostolic Church.
people/cyril-of-jerusalem/summary: Bishop of Jerusalem (c.350–386), several times exiled during the Arian controversies, whose Catechetical Lectures (c.350) and Mystagogical Catecheses (attributed to him or his successor John) give a vivid picture of baptism, chrismation and Eucharist in 4th-century Jerusalem, including a strong realist teaching on the change of bread and wine and the invocation (epiclesis) of the Spirit.
people/cyril-of-jerusalem/keyIdeas/0: Mystagogy: explaining the sacraments after initiation
people/cyril-of-jerusalem/keyIdeas/1: Real change of the eucharistic elements
people/paul-vi/summary: Giovanni Battista Montini, pope from 1963 to 1978, who carried the Second Vatican Council to completion, promulgating Lumen Gentium, Unitatis Redintegratio and other documents, implemented liturgical reform, met Patriarch Athenagoras (mutual lifting of the 1054 excommunications, 1965), defended transubstantiation (Mysterium Fidei, 1965) and issued Humanae Vitae (1968).
people/florence-li-tim-oi/summary: Hong Kong-born Anglican who, ordained priest by Bishop Ronald Hall in 1944 to serve Macau’s Christians during the Japanese occupation, became the first woman priest in the Anglican Communion. Under pressure she ceased to exercise her priesthood after the war; she later suffered re-education during the Cultural Revolution, and her orders were publicly recognised again in Hong Kong in 1971 and in Canada, where she died.
people/florence-li-tim-oi/keyIdeas/0: First woman ordained priest in the Anglican Communion (1944)
people/florence-li-tim-oi/keyIdeas/1: Faithfulness under persecution in Communist China
people/johann-agricola/summary: Eisleben-born pupil and colleague of Luther whose insistence that repentance flows from the gospel, not the preaching of the law, sparked the first antinomian controversies: with Melanchthon over the Saxon Visitation Articles (1527) and with Luther himself (1537–40). He recanted in 1540, became court preacher in Berlin and helped draft the Augsburg Interim (1548).
people/johann-agricola/keyIdeas/0: Repentance is worked by the gospel, not the law
people/johann-agricola/keyIdeas/1: The law belongs in the courthouse, not the pulpit
people/johann-agricola/keyIdeas/2: Opposition to the Visitation Articles of 1527
